newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU report on regional policies delayed.
newsitem.headline: EU report on regional policies delayed.

text.p: An in-depth European Commission report on regional policies in the European Union has been delayed, probably for a week, a Commission source said on Tuesday.
The postponement was forced by a need to make a "few minor changes" to the report, which is expected to show that EU regional policies have helped to narrow the gap between poor and rich EU members.
There were no problems in substance, the source added.
Because of this, EU Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies has cancelled her press conference which was scheduled for 1115 GMT on Wednesday.
The report is expected to show that progress has been made in reducing differences in living standards but also that some policy changes will be needed.
"Regional disparities have been reduced and the poorer member states have caught up," one Commission official said earlier, referring to Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Spain.

The report -- which covers the 10 years up to 1993 -- looks at trends in cohesion between member states, regions and social groups and at how and whether member states' policies and EU policies have contributed to boost regional development.
It will provide a basis for a future look at how the structural funds will be affected by the enlargement towards poorer eastern and central European countries.
It will be the first time such a report has been made and concrete work on enlargement and regional policy would start only after the report is published.
Many fear that eastern enlargement will be a costly affair, not least because of expected massive needs of regional support to the new members.

Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies said recently that the EU could bring in new members from eastern and central Europe without raising the budget contributions from EU states that have already been agreed.

But she added that it would not be possible to take in new members for free, saying EU support for poor regions may increase by as much as 30 percent in the period 2000-2006 compared with the previous seven years.
The structural funds are the EU's primary vehicle for promoting economic and social balance and reducing regional disparities among the 15 member states.

For the 1994-1999 period the funds' allocation amounts to 141 billion European currency units ($179 billion). The amount allocated to the funds from the EU budget have has increased to 35.7 percent from 17.5 percent in 1988.

In addition, a Cohesion Fund with a total of 13.6 billion Ecus for the 1994-99 period complements the structural funds for those countries whose gross domestic product is below 90 percent of the EU average -- Spain, Greece, Portugal and Ireland.
